title: The bridge that learned to walk
text: London's Millennium Bridge opened on 10 June 2000, {{1}} two thousand people across the Thames, and closed two days later. The problem was not the design's {{2}} but a subtlety of human movement: as crowds walk, they sway slightly, and a sideways-swaying bridge {{3}} them to synchronise their steps, which sways it more — a feedback loop engineers now call synchronous lateral excitation. The {{4}} was elegant: thirty-seven viscous dampers and fifty-two tuned mass dampers, gadgets that {{5}} the sideways motion before it could recruit the crowd. The bridge reopened in 2002 and has been faultless since, its {{6}} now a textbook case in engineering courses worldwide. The episode {{7}} a wider truth about complex systems: each component behaved exactly as specified, yet the combination {{8}} behaviour no one had predicted, because nobody had specified the people. Modern engineers model crowds the way their predecessors modelled wind — as a living load with opinions of its own.
